title: The Group Project That Counted Invisible Work
passage:
A high school history course required students to complete a four-person research project. Each group produced a presentation, source list, and short report. At the end of the term, complaints appeared. Some students said one person had done nearly all the work. Others argued that teachers could not see important tasks such as organizing meetings, checking sources, or helping classmates revise unclear sections. The final product showed what the group had made, but not how the work had been distributed.

The teacher considered requiring students to record every minute spent on the project. That seemed objective, yet it created new problems. Time is not the same as contribution. A student might spend three hours searching inefficiently while another finds a strong source in twenty minutes. Detailed tracking could also turn collaboration into competition over recorded effort.

Instead, the class tested a contribution log based on tasks and decisions. Once a week, each group listed what had been completed, who had taken primary responsibility, who had supported the task, and what still needed attention. The log included categories such as research, writing, visual design, scheduling, source checking, rehearsal, and conflict resolution. Students could add categories when necessary.

The first logs revealed that some work really had been invisible. In one group, a quiet student had contributed little text but had checked every quotation against the original source and found two errors. In another, one student scheduled meetings and combined separate slides into a consistent presentation. At the same time, the logs made genuine imbalance easier to see. A few students repeatedly appeared only as minor supporters without taking responsibility for any substantial task.

The teacher did not use the logs to calculate a mechanical percentage for each student. Instead, they were one piece of evidence alongside the final work, peer comments, and short individual reflections. Groups were also asked to review their own distribution halfway through the project. If one person was overloaded, tasks could be reassigned before the deadline rather than only criticized afterward.

A new issue emerged: students sometimes described small actions in exaggerated language to make their contribution appear larger. The teacher responded by asking for concrete outcomes. ‘Helped with research’ became ‘found two newspaper articles and summarized their arguments.’ Specific descriptions were easier for group members to confirm and more useful for planning.

By the next project, complaints about unfairness decreased but did not disappear. Collaboration still involved judgment. A brilliant idea could matter greatly even if it took only a minute, while routine editing might require hours. The school decided that no record could convert teamwork into a perfectly precise number.

The value of the log was different. It made roles discussable. Students learned that visible production—writing a paragraph or speaking during the presentation—was only part of collective work. Coordination, checking, listening, and repair could be equally important. At the same time, calling work ‘invisible’ could not become an excuse for doing very little. The group needed evidence that the task had actually helped the project.

The teacher's goal shifted from measuring every contribution exactly to creating enough transparency for students to adjust while the work was still happening. Fairness did not come from a perfect formula. It came from making expectations clear, naming different kinds of contribution, and giving groups a chance to correct imbalance before it hardened into resentment.
translation:
高校の歴史授業で四人組の研究発表を行ったところ、『一人に仕事が集中した』『先生には会議調整や資料確認のような見えない仕事が分からない』という不満が出ました。完成物だけでは仕事の分担過程が見えませんでした。

教師は作業時間をすべて記録する案も考えましたが、時間と貢献度は同じではありません。三時間非効率に探す人と、二十分で良い資料を見つける人を単純比較できず、細かな時間競争になる危険もあります。

そこで毎週、完了した作業、主担当、支援者、残課題を記録する『貢献ログ』を試しました。研究、執筆、デザイン、日程調整、出典確認、練習、対立調整などの項目を用意しました。

ログを見ると、文章は少なくても全引用を原典と照合し誤りを二つ見つけた生徒や、会議調整とスライド統合を担当していた生徒がいました。一方で、いつも小さな補助だけで大きな責任を持たない生徒も明確になりました。

教師はログを機械的な割合計算には使わず、完成物、相互評価、個人振り返りと合わせて判断しました。途中で分担を見直し、一人に負担が集中していれば締切前に修正できるようにしました。

小さな作業を大げさに書く例も出たため、『研究を手伝った』ではなく『新聞記事を二本見つけ、主張を要約した』のような具体的成果を書くようにしました。

不公平感は減りましたが、完全には消えませんでした。一瞬の優れた発想が大きな価値を持つこともあれば、地道な編集に何時間もかかることもあります。協働を完全な数字にはできません。

ログの価値は、役割を話し合えるようにしたことでした。文章や発表だけでなく、調整、確認、聞くこと、修正も重要です。ただし『見えない仕事』という言葉をほとんど働かない言い訳にはできません。

目標は全員の貢献を完全に測ることではなく、作業中に十分な透明性を作り、偏りを修正できるようにすることへ変わりました。公平さは完璧な公式ではなく、期待を明確にし、さまざまな貢献を言葉にすることで生まれました。
